scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that values consensus while insisting leaders keep their ideals; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Politics often forces a choice between sticking to principles and reaching a workable deal.
Some people recommend that politicians should pursue common ground and reasonable consensus rather than chase elusive ideals.
I agree that compromise is often necessary, but I believe politicians must not abandon their ideals altogether.
First, seeking common ground is often the only way to get things done in government.
In a divided society, no single group can have everything it wants, so compromise becomes essential.
For example, a budget or a peace deal usually passes only when opposing sides agree to give up something.
This shows that reasonable consensus can turn endless argument into real and lasting progress.
Politicians who refuse ever to compromise often achieve nothing but deadlock and anger.
Working toward agreement also helps hold a divided nation peacefully together.
For these reasons, the pursuit of common ground is a genuine political virtue.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why ideals are still needed

sentences.text: Second, however, abandoning all ideals in the name of consensus would be a serious mistake.
Ideals give politics its direction and remind leaders what they are actually trying to achieve.
Consider reformers who refused to compromise on justice and slowly changed unfair laws that most people once accepted.
Such courage shows that some ideals are worth defending even when easy agreement is impossible.
A leader with no ideals may chase agreement for its own sake and drift along without purpose.
Real progress sometimes requires holding firm to a principle until others can be persuaded.
Ideals, then, should guide the search for consensus rather than be thrown away in it.
In conclusion, politicians are right to seek common ground, since compromise makes government work.
But they should never surrender the ideals that give their work meaning and direction.
The best leaders pursue practical consensus while staying true to the principles worth fighting for.
